title.en: The countless Rudras: their bows unstrung, homage in every quarter

summary: Ten ṛks and a closing yajus. The ṛks name the Rudras in their thousands — on the earth, in the atmosphere, below the earth, in heaven, in trees, as lords of spirits, in food and drink, on the roads, at the fords and in every quarter — and say of each that their bows are unstrung a thousand yojanas away; Sāyaṇa supplies this refrain to ṛks 2–9, which are half-lines in the Saṃhitā. The yajus salutes the Rudras of earth, sky and heaven, whose arrows are food, wind and rain, with joined hands to all ten quarters, and gives the enemy into their jaws; Sāyaṇa reads it as three yajus for three offerings, and ends the anuvāka with the Brāhmaṇa’s account of the whole Śatarudrīya offering at the building of the fire altar.

vyakarana.note: Vedic present 1st pl. of tan ‘stretch’ (8th class), formed without the class sign -u- and with the Vedic ending -masi (classical tanumaḥ). With ava, standing apart: ‘we unstring’.
An adverb in -śas, distributive: ‘by thousands’. Sāyaṇa takes it of kinds (सहस्रश इति जात्युक्तिः) and sahasrāṇi of number.

Locative of the distance at which the bows are laid down: ‘at a thousand yojanas’.

translation.literal: Thousands by thousands, the Rudras who [are] upon the earth — of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows.
translation.readable: Of the Rudras who are upon the earth, thousands upon thousands, we unstring the bows a thousand yojanas away.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the anuvāka gives the remaining ṛks and yajus, and first ten ṛks («तत्राऽऽदौ दशसंख्याका ऋचः»). sahasrāṇi gives the number of the Rudras, sahasraśaḥ their kinds («सहस्रश इति जात्युक्तिः»): the troops of Vināyaka and the rest are kinds, «ते सर्वेऽपि रुद्रविशेषाः», all of them particular Rudras, and each kind numbers many thousands of forms. ‘Their bows we set down, the strings slackened (अवततज्याकानि स्थापयामः), in a region a thousand yojanas away from us (सहस्रयोजनव्यवहितदेशे).’
units.reflection: Nothing here is destroyed. The bows are only unstrung and put far away — the distance itself is the request.

words.meaning: in the flood, in the ocean
words.context: Sāyaṇa: like a great ocean (महासमुद्रसदृशे), said of the atmosphere
Sāyaṇa: particular forms of Rudra

sandhi.rule: i before a dissimilar vowel becomes y (iko yaṇ aci, P. 6.1.77)
a final e or o absorbs a following a, marked by avagraha (eṅaḥ padāntād ati, P. 6.1.109)
-āḥ loses its visarga before a voiced sound or a vowel

vyakarana.note: In apposition to antarikṣe: the atmosphere is called ‘this great flood’ (Sāyaṇa: like a great ocean).
The plural of Bhava, a name of Rudra, for the many Rudras of the mid-region; the relative ye of ṛk 1 is understood (Sāyaṇa: ये सन्ति).
Postposition with the locatives: ‘in this great flood, the atmosphere’. The ṛk is a half-line; its second half is supplied from ṛk 1 (see the traditional note).

translation.literal: In this great flood, the atmosphere, the Bhavas [who are] in [it] — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: The Bhavas who dwell in this great flood, the atmosphere: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: in this visible great atmosphere, vast and like the great ocean (महासमुद्रसदृशे प्रौढेऽन्तरिक्षे), dwell the Bhavas, particular forms of Rudra («भवा रुद्रमूर्तिविशेषा ये सन्ति»). This ṛk and the seven after it are single half-lines in the Saṃhitā. To each Sāyaṇa supplies the second half of the first ṛk, by anuṣaṅga: «तेषां सहस्रयोजन इत्याद्युक्ता २१४१ र्थमुत्तरार्थं द्वितीयादिषु नवप्रान्तास्वृक्ष, अनुषज्जते» — so the printed bhāṣya reads, interrupted by the page number २१४१; it says that the latter half stated [in the first ṛk], teṣāṃ sahasrayojane …, is carried over (anuṣaṅga) to the ṛks from the second to the ninth. And the half is recited again in the tenth ṛk for this very reason: «तदनुषङ्गद्योतनायैव दशम्यामृचि पुनः पठितम्» — ‘it is read again in the tenth ṛk precisely to show this anuṣaṅga’.

vyakarana.note: An adverb, ‘below’, with kṣamācarāḥ: ‘moving below, in the earth’.
The plural of Śarva, a name of Rudra, for the many Rudras below the earth; the refrain of ṛk 1 is supplied.

translation.literal: Blue-necked, white-throated, the Śarvas moving below, in the earth — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: The blue-necked, white-throated Śarvas who roam beneath the earth: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: blue in one part of the neck and white in another — «ग्रीवायाम् एकस्मिन् प्रदेशे नीलवर्णा नीलग्रीवाः प्रदेशान्तरे श्वेतवर्णाः शितिकण्ठाः». Such are the Śarvas, particular forms of Rudra (शर्वा रुद्रमूर्तिविशेषाः), who move ‘beneath the earth, in the nether worlds’ (भूमेरधस्तात्पातालेषु संचरन्ति). He closes with «तेषामित्यादि पूर्ववत्»: ‘teṣām …’ follows as before.

vyakarana.note: Past participle of śri ‘lean, rest’ with upa, taking the accusative divam: ‘resting upon heaven’ (MW: ‘leaning upon’).
Acc. sg. of div / dyu ‘heaven’, the goal of upaśritāḥ.

translation.literal: Blue-necked, white-throated, the Rudras resting upon heaven — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: The blue-necked, white-throated Rudras who dwell in heaven: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa adds only that these Rudras «दिवमुपश्रिताः स्वर्गे वर्तमानाः», ‘resting on heaven’, that is, dwelling in heaven; the colours are as in the previous ṛk, and the refrain is supplied.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (upamāna: the first member is the standard of comparison)
samasa.meaning: tawny like young grass (MW: ṣaṣpiñjara, for śaṣpa-piñjara; the TS spells it sas-)

vyakarana.note: śaṣpa ‘young grass’ + piñjara ‘tawny, yellowish-red’, with one syllable pa lost (MW: ‘for śaṣpa-p°’); the Taittirīya spells the first member sas-.
The relative clause has no main clause of its own: the refrain of ṛk 1 (teṣām … tanmasi) completes it.

translation.literal: Who [are] in the trees, yellowish like young grass, blue-necked, deep-red — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: Those in the trees, tawny like young grass, blue-necked and deep-red: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: as Rudras dwell in the worlds, so they dwell in trees («यथा लोकेष्ववस्थिता रुद्रास्तथा वृक्षेष्ववस्थिताः»). Some are saspiñjara, tawny like young grass (शष्पवद्); some blue-necked; others «विशेषेण रक्तवर्णाः», especially red. ‘Those who are such — teṣām …’ (तेषामित्यादि).

words.context: Sāyaṇa: hosts with hidden bodies who trouble men
Sāyaṇa: with shaven heads
Sāyaṇa: जटाबन्धोपेताः, with matted locks

sandhi.rule: final m before a vowel stays m and is written together with it
-aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)
visarga before k is written as the jihvāmūlīya ᳵ (P. 8.3.37 allows it)

vyakarana.note: Vedic nom. pl. in -āsaḥ (classical viśikhāḥ). MW: viśikha ‘devoid of the top-knot or tuft of hair’.
Genitive with adhipatayaḥ: ‘the overlords of the bhūtas’.

translation.literal: Who [are] the overlords of beings, without top-knots, with braided hair — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: The lords of the spirits, shaven-headed and with braided hair: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa takes bhūta here as the hosts who, with hidden bodies, trouble men: «भूतशब्देनान्तर्हितशरीराः सन्तो मनुष्योपद्रवकारिणो गणविशेषा उच्यन्ते». Of the Rudras who rule them, some are viśikha, with shaven heads (the printed gloss is damaged here), and others «कपर्दिनो जटाबन्धोपेताः», with matted locks; then the refrain (तेषामित्यादि).

Sāyaṇa: in drinks such as milk and water

words.gram: pres. part. of √pā ‘drink’, m. acc. pl.

sandhi.rule: final -e before a is kept and the a is not elided — the Vedic option, as namo astu
-aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)

vyakarana.note: vi + vyadh, present stem vidhya- (4th class, with samprasāraṇa): ‘pierce through, wound’.
Acc. pl. of pibat, the present participle of pā (stem piba-), with janān: ‘people as they drink’.

translation.literal: Who pierce people in [their] foods [and], in [their] cups, as they drink — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: Those who wound people in their food, and in their cups as they drink: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: these Rudras stay hidden (गूढत्वेनावस्थिताः) in the food that is eaten and afflict people, for instance by an imbalance of the bodily elements («विशेषेण धातुवैषम्यादिना बाधन्ते»); in the same way, hidden in drinks such as milk and water (क्षीरोदकादिषु), they wound those who drink; then the refrain.

samasa.meaning: bearers of food; MW: ‘bringing or procuring plenty of food’

vyakarana.note: Gen. pl. of pathin (weak stem path-), going with pathirakṣayaḥ: ‘guardians of the paths’ — Sāyaṇa: of all paths.

aila, from irā ‘food, refreshment’: ‘plenty of food’. The second member -bṛda Sāyaṇa takes from bhṛ ‘bear’ (aila-bhṛt becoming ailabṛda); MW gives the compound the sense ‘bringing or procuring plenty of food’.
Nom. pl. of yavyudh. MW records it as a spelling of yavīyudh ‘eager to fight’, from the intensive of yudh. Sāyaṇa analyses it as yu ‘enemy’ + yudh: ‘who fight with enemies’.

translation.literal: Who [are] the guardians of the paths, of the roads, bringers of food, eager fighters — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: The guardians of every road, who bring food and are eager to fight: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: pathirakṣayaḥ are protectors of the paths, worldly and Vedic (लौकिकवैदिकमार्गाणां रक्षकाः), and the genitive pathām says they guard not some paths but all: «नात्र केषांचिदेव मार्गाणां किंतु सर्वेषां पथां ते च रक्षकाः». He derives ailabṛda from irā, food: its mass is aira, aira is aila, and those who bear it are ailabhṛt — «ऐलभृत एवैलबृदा अन्नप्रदानेन पोषका इत्यर्थः», ‘who nourish by giving food’. yavyudh he takes from yu, the enemy («यौति मिश्री भवति विरोधं करोतीति यु, शत्रुः»): «युभिः शत्रुभिः सह युध्यन्तीति यव्युधः» — they fight with enemies and so ward off what is unwelcome to us; then the refrain.

flags.note: yavyudh: MW takes it as a spelling of yavīyudh ‘eager to fight’ (from the intensive of yudh); Sāyaṇa as ‘fighting with enemies’ (yu ‘enemy’). The translation keeps the dictionary sense; the word table gives both.
ailabṛda: the sense ‘bringing plenty of food’ is shared by MW and Sāyaṇa, but the formation of -bṛda (Sāyaṇa: from bhṛ) is not certain.

words.context: Sāyaṇa: to protect them
Sāyaṇa: carrying sharp-pointed knives
Sāyaṇa: खड्ग-युक्ताः, armed with swords

sandhi.rule: -aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes -o (P. 6.1.114)

vyakarana.note: sṛka ‘arrow, spear’ (MW) with the possessive suffix -vat, the a lengthened before it (sṛkā-vat).
pra + car with the accusative tīrthāni: ‘go about the fords’. The pañcāśat mark [26] stands between tīrthāni and pracaranti; no sandhi is made across it.

translation.literal: Who roam about the fords, armed with spears, with quivers — [of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows].
translation.readable: Those who go about the sacred fords, armed with spears and quivers: [their bows we unstring, a thousand yojanas away].

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: these Rudras go about the tīrthas, such as Kāśī and Prayāga, to protect them (रक्षितुं प्रचरन्ति). Some carry sṛkas, «सृकाश् छुरिका हस्ते धार्यमाणास्», sharp-pointed knives held in the hand; others are niṣaṅgin, which he glosses here as ‘armed with swords’ (खड्ग-युक्ताः); then the refrain (तेषामित्यादि).

flags.note: niṣaṅgin: MW ‘having a quiver (or sword?)’; Sāyaṇa here: ‘armed with swords’. The translation keeps ‘quivers’.

Perfect middle 3rd pl. of sthā with vi, ‘have spread out over’, with the accusative diśaḥ.

translation.literal: The Rudras who, so many and more, have spread out over the quarters — of them, at a thousand yojanas, we unstring the bows.
translation.readable: Of the Rudras, as many as these and more, who have spread through all the quarters, we unstring the bows a thousand yojanas away.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa: the Rudras as many as the preceding ṛks have named, and others more numerous still (भूयांसः), «सर्वा दिशः प्रविश्य स्थिताः», who have entered and stand in all the quarters. He has already explained why the second half returns here: «तदनुषङ्गद्योतनायैव दशम्यामृचि पुनः पठितम्», to show that it is carried over to the ṛks before. In the rite, the third of the three portions in which the Śatarudrīya is offered ends with this ṛk: «नमः प्रतरणाय चेत्यारभ्य य एतावन्तश्चेत्यृचा सहितस्तृतीयो भागः».

vyakarana.note: Predicate of annam, vātaḥ, varṣam: ‘whose arrows [are] food, wind, rain’.

prācīḥ, dakṣiṇāḥ, pratīcīḥ, udīcīḥ, ūrdhvāḥ are feminine plurals with no noun expressed; with daśa ‘ten’ they describe the salutation. Sāyaṇa understands the ten fingers of the joined hands (दशाङ्गुलयः).
Loc. sg. of div ‘heaven’.
The second te (‘they’) has no verb of its own: the sentence turns to the enemy, ‘whom we hate and who hates us, him I put in your jaws’. Sāyaṇa reads it with the speakers (ते च वयं …).
Enclitic gen. pl. of yuṣmad (for yuṣmākam): ‘your’, addressed to the Rudras.
Present of dviṣ (2nd class): dviṣmaḥ 1st pl., dveṣṭi 3rd sg. (guṇa in the strong form).
Present 1st sg. of dhā (3rd class, reduplicated): ‘I place’.

translation.literal: Homage to the Rudras who [are] on the earth, who [are] in the atmosphere, who [are] in heaven, whose arrows [are] food, wind, rain. To them ten eastward, ten southward, ten westward, ten northward, ten upward; to them homage. Let them be gracious to us. They — whom we hate and who hates us, him I place in your jaws.
translation.readable: Homage to the Rudras who are on the earth, in the atmosphere and in heaven, whose arrows are food, wind and rain. To them, ten [fingers] to the east, ten to the south, ten to the west, ten to the north, ten upward; to them, homage. May they be gracious to us. The one we hate and the one who hates us — him I place in your jaws.

units.traditional: Sāyaṇa reads this as three yajus, by the three worlds and the three arrows: «अत्र पृथिव्यादिलोकभेदादिषुभेदाच्च यजुस्त्रयं द्रष्टव्यम्». The first runs from namo rudrebhyaḥ through ye pṛthivyām and yeṣām annam iṣavaḥ; «येऽन्तरिक्षे येषां वात इषव इति द्वितीयो मन्त्रः»; «ये दिवि येषां वर्षमिषव इति तृतीयो मन्त्रः»; and «तेभ्यो दश प्राचीरित्यादि सर्वत्र समानम्», the rest is the same in all three. The Saṃhitā gives them as one passage, and it is analysed here as it stands. Food is the arrow of the Rudras on earth, who harm by leading people to eat what is unwholesome (अपथ्यान्नभक्षणे) or to steal for food; wind, of those in the atmosphere, who «तीव्रेण वायुना रोगानुत्पाद्य हिंसन्ति», cause disease by violent winds; rain, of those in heaven: «वर्षमेवेषवोऽतिवृष्ट्यनावृष्टिभ्यां प्राणिनो हिंसन्ति», they harm creatures by too much rain or none. ‘Ten eastward’ describes the salutation: «प्राङ्मुखत्वेनाञ्चलिकरणे दशाङ्गुलयः प्रागग्रा भवन्ति» — when the hands are joined facing east, the ten fingers point east; and so for the other quarters. Each time ‘homage to them, and may they make us happy’ (मृडयन्तु सुखयन्तु). The enemy whom we hate though he keeps silent, and who hates us though we keep silent, is placed ‘in your gaping mouth’ (विदारितास्ये), O Rudras. For the rite, Sāyaṇa quotes the Brāhmaṇa: these yajus are three further offerings, «उत्तरा आहुतीर्जुहोति षट्संपद्यन्ते षड्वा ऋतव ऋतुभिरेवैनँ शमयति» — with the threefold Śatarudrīya they make six; the seasons are six, and by the seasons he appeases him — and the sacrificer is made to recite them («ता यजमानं वाचयति»). His summary verse: «नमो रुद्रेभ्य इत्येष पृथिव्यादिविभेदतः। त्रेधा भिन्नस्ततो होमे षण्मन्त्रा इह कीर्तिताः».

flags.note: corrections.json (N11.11, W2 error): the second witness reads प्रातीचीः; the base witness’s प्रतीचीः (pratīcī, the west, beside prācī, dakṣiṇā, udīcī) is kept.

The text is one yajus in the Saṃhitā; Sāyaṇa, following the ritual, divides it into three mantras (ye pṛthivyām … annam, ye 'ntarikṣe … vātaḥ, ye divi … varṣam), each completed by tebhyo daśa prācīḥ … The analysis follows the Saṃhitā.

The second te is construed loosely (an anacoluthon) in the translation; Sāyaṇa takes it with the speakers, ‘and we, [having saluted the Rudras] …’. The feminine plurals prācīḥ … ūrdhvāḥ have no noun in the text; ‘fingers’ is Sāyaṇa’s.
